Information can be health. Most of what we know never arrives in a form anyone can
act on, and that is a solvable problem.
:::

## Where do people go for health information?

A grandfather is closing in on eighty. He lives with his daughter and her family,
three kids, three generations in one house, and whatever else the day did to them,
they eat dinner together. Around that table, every one of them is being taught
about health all day long, by somebody. Never the same somebody.

The youngest is ten, and her somebody is the feed. The feed is gorgeous: rainbow
cakes, foot-tall cookies, candy sculpted into art, because it is art, and none of
it is food anyone needs. Between the cakes she is sold skincare in packaging she
adores, full of ingredients she cannot pronounce. Ask her what those ingredients
do, on her face or inside her body, and she could not begin to tell you. She does
not care, and neither, really, does the family, because all of them spend every
day walking around a world where this is what normal looks like.

Her brother is in his early teens, spent a couple of years heavier than he wanted
to be, and loves video games more than almost anything. His somebody is nobody:
no channel anywhere is aimed at him. Whatever he comes to believe about food and
his own body, he will assemble alone, out of whatever drifts past.

Their mother's somebody is the wellness internet, which sells certainty by the
serving: a banana a day can cure her period symptoms, this tea for that hormone,
always one special food away from fixed.

The grandfather's somebody, at least, went to school for this. He got a diagnosis
and fifteen minutes. Blood pressure. Less salt, less red meat. He grew up on
Philly cheesesteaks and Sunday meatballs, London broil when there was something
worth celebrating. None of the advice is wrong, exactly. It just arrives as a
list of subtractions from the person he has been his whole life, with nothing
about what a good week of eating could look like instead.

All of it comes home to one table. Four people, four channels, shaped by different
generations and different norms, and each channel borrows its authority from the
same place. The skincare ad gestures at studies, the banana post does, the doctor
does. The word being borrowed is science. Some care is owed here, because science
is not one source of truth, and the honest version of it never claimed to be. It
is a way of earning answers slowly and in public, and the highest-quality truths
people have ever had about health have historically come from that slow, public
earning. Which is exactly what makes the name worth borrowing.

Here is the strange part. Not one person at that table could tell you how that
earning works. They trust science because school told them to, and the trust
outlived the understanding. That is not their failure, and it is not quite an
accident either.

Not an accident, because the institutions that produce the knowledge answer to
the next publication rather than to anyone at this table. Left alone with that
incentive, a field can group-think its way into an ivory tower built on a
comfortable lie: that science is unbiased by nature. It is not. Every algorithm
carries somebody's judgment inside it, and so does every risk score and every
model. Hiding the judgment while the walls stayed high is how trust and
understanding came apart. Science has been inaccessible for generations, and by
now it is actively designed out of daily life, while the feed, which answers to
their attention every single day, is designed in.

So what would a channel designed in their favor have to get right? For any of
them, information worth having needs four things to be true at the same time. It
has to be **accurate**, or it is worse than nothing. **Actionable**, or it
changes no one's Tuesday. **Accessible**, or it reaches only people who already had
good options. And **fun**, because attention is the currency and nobody finishes
something dutiful.

| The channel | Accurate | Actionable | Accessible | Fun |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The ten-year-old's feed** | Rarely, and paid by the click | Instantly | Never off | It is the entire product |
| **The mother's wellness marketing** | No, and accountable to no one | Very | Everywhere she looks | Yes |
| **The grandfather's fifteen minutes** | Yes, for medicine | "Less salt" is not a plan | Only with a doctor and a diagnosis | No |

The boy has no row, because nothing is aimed at him at all, which is its own answer
to all four. Nobody at that table gets all four at once. Everything real gets built
on the assumption that people will tolerate boring if it is true, and they will
not, and then we call that a motivation problem.

There is one more absence at that table, easy to miss. Nobody in this family has
ever sat down with a dietitian or a health coach. None of them even thought to,
and that is no fault of theirs. The one somebody with a diploma on the wall gets
fifteen minutes, and in fifteen minutes the referral to people who could actually
help never comes up. Part of that is time. Part is social standing: physicians are
educated people who make a lot of money, and everything below them on that ladder
reads as less than expert. And the biggest part is belief: if our most trusted
health experts do not really believe that help with food and habit moves health,
why would they ever think to point toward it?

Now imagine the channels stay exactly where they are and only what flows through
them changes. The ten-year-old follows creators her own age who are genuinely wise
about health and every bit as fun as the cakes. Her brother discovers that somebody
finally built a channel that talks to him where he already lives. Their mother gets
a way to read the quality of her family's whole diet at once, so the weekly shop
turns into the place she teaches her kids what she is learning. And the grandfather
hears something no one has thought to tell him: his fruit and vegetables are
already enough, his blood pressure is doing remarkably well, and the best thing he
can spend effort on now is moving more and building up his legs, because old age is
a winter, and he will want the strength to walk through it.

Same family, same table, same channels. Different information. That is the whole
project, and the rest of this page is about what it takes to build it honestly.

## Discovery and delivery are one loop

I sat in an audience once while a room applauded an elder academic, and the applause
was deserved. He had carried a compound the whole way, bench to pharmacy shelf, and
he had the scars to show for it. Twenty years, start to finish. I clapped along with
everyone else. It took me a while to notice what we were celebrating: a twenty-year
cycle, held up as the achievement of a career, and nobody in that room found the
number strange.

The number is, if anything, on the fast side. Clinical development alone runs a
[median of 8.3 years](https://doi.org/10.1038/d41573-021-00190-9) from first dose in
a human to approval, and the longer arc, from a promising laboratory finding to the
clinical work that carries it, has a [median of 24
years](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1160622). Most findings never make the trip at
all. Of [101 basic-science papers](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0002-9343(03)00013-5)
that promised a new treatment, twenty-some years later five had reached licensed
clinical use, and one was in wide practice.

The supply side has no such trouble. PubMed now holds [more than 40 million
citations](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and took in over 1.5 million in a single
year, and the scientific literature as a whole
[doubles](https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-021-00903-w) about every seventeen. One
registry lists [1,382 cardiovascular prediction
models](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCOUTCOMES.121.007858), of which 58 percent have
never been tested on anyone outside the population that produced them. More than a
hundred [nutrient profiling systems](https://doi.org/10.1093/advances/nmy045) decide
what counts as a healthy food in government policy. We are extremely good at making
more.

A good deal of that effort never reaches the science at all. [I ran the arithmetic
once](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7414791698649645057/):
ten hours of formatting per paper, roughly five thousand papers published a day, and
the field burns something like fifty thousand hours a day rewrapping its findings to
suit one journal or the next. Both inputs are estimates, though PubMed's own intake
puts the daily count in that neighborhood. Fifty thousand hours a day on the shape of
the container, while the question of whether anything inside it reached a person goes
unfunded and unasked.

Ask that question and the answer stays flat. Adults in the United States
were getting [about 55 percent of recommended
care](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa022615) in 2003, and the
[60-30-10](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-020-01563-4) pattern (roughly 60 percent of
care matching the evidence, 30 percent waste, 10 percent harm) has held for three
decades. Discovery compounds. Delivery holds flat. We keep opening new channels for
finding things out and almost none for finding out whether the last thing worked.

That is not a paradox and it is not anybody's failure. Discovery never ends, and it
should not. The honest position on almost any specific person is that most of what
we would need to know about them is still unknown, and will be after another million
papers. Anyone who tells you the science is settled at the level of your actual life
is selling something.

What it is selling, usually, is a number that never went back for a second look.
Everyone in this field quotes seventeen years as the lag between evidence and
practice. It comes from [a chapter
published in 2000](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0038-1637943) that assembled the figure
from nine clinical areas, and one of its inputs was
[wrong](https://doi.org/10.1177/2381468317734527) by a factor of three: it assumed
one in five people with diabetes got a foot exam when the real rate was closer to
three in five. A [review of 23 lag estimates](https://doi.org/10.1258/jrsm.2011.110180)
found them ranging from under one year to more than 28, measuring different things at
different points, and concluded that the existing knowledge was of limited use. The
seventeen years gets repeated anyway, a quarter-century on. A field that measures its
own translation lag with a number nobody ever went back and revised is telling you
exactly how much it values the return trip.

So the work is not to wait for certainty. It is to translate what we have carefully,
say how sure we are, and keep listening for what comes back. Discovery and delivery
are one loop. A study becomes a guideline, a guideline becomes something a person
actually does, what happens next gets observed, and what comes back decides which
question is worth asking next. Each half steers the other, and the quality of the
whole thing depends on something unglamorous: whether we can orchestrate science
toward questions that matter, and carry the answers back to people in a shape they
can act on. Discovery is endless; the bottleneck is translation, and it is a pity
that delivery is still this bad.

One reason it is this bad is that the return edge is missing. [Mapping the
organizations that sit between evidence and
action](../ai-for-science-map/), the last thing anyone does is revise: find out the
thing is not working, and stop. Almost nothing occupies that stage, and the reason is
structural rather than lazy. Stopping needs a rule set in advance, a rule needs to
know whether the thing is working, and that needs a benefit signal. [We built
surveillance for harm and almost none for
benefit](../we-measure-harm-we-mean-benefit/), so nothing tells you it is working,
so no stopping rule can be written, so nothing flows back into what gets studied
next.

That is why the incentive structures that produce fifty competing dietary indices
were never going to produce one useful answer. Nothing downstream was ever going to
tell them which of the fifty was worth having. The argument over what counts as
ultraprocessed is the shiniest current example: enormous political and scientific
capital spent on a definition, while the person holding a box in a grocery aisle
gets no closer to knowing what to do, and no signal returns from that aisle to say
so.

There is one more job, and it is the one everybody skips. Sometimes a person brings
a real problem and the honest answer is that nobody knows yet. Not "here are five
studies," not a confident guess dressed up in numbers. Nobody knows. A system that
can only speak when it has an answer goes quiet exactly when someone needs it most,
and silence gets filled by whoever is willing to sound certain. Saying plainly that
a question is unresolved, showing what is actually known around the edges of it, and
staying with the person while they decide anyway, is worth as much as any answer.
Most of the honest ground in health looks like that.

## Why nobody built it

Universities generate the knowledge that ends up in our books and our schools. Ask
almost any researcher how it is going and you will hear some version of just
surviving. The work gets produced and then it goes nowhere in particular, because
nothing orchestrates it toward the questions that matter, and articles pile up in
the tens of thousands where no family will ever look.

There has never been a real source of quality health information and delivery
because there has never been an incentive to build one. Not in medicine. Not in
health care. Not in the food industry. Not in prestigious academic institutions.
Nowhere.

Nowhere includes the classroom. There is no recognized field of study called
health engineering, so we are not training anyone to even conceive of this
problem, let alone solve it. We are training more tissue engineers, more
physiologists, more environmental scientists, more statisticians, more ear, nose,
and throat doctors, more influencers, more politicians specializing in
definitions of ultraprocessed food. All of them useful, some of them amazing, and
still the gap remains: somewhere in the mix, somebody has to stop specializing
and learn across the specialties. Isn't generalizable knowledge supposed to be
the whole point of science?

## How I got here

I was one of those tissue engineers. I spent years building multicellular experimental
models of inflammation, regeneration, and disease. Somewhere in there I became
convinced the real problem was not our ability to generate health knowledge. It was
our almost complete inability to orchestrate that generation toward questions
worth asking, and then to consolidate and deliver what comes back.

So I moved sideways, into nutritional epidemiology, and then into building. I have
published in the field, worked with people who know far more than I do, and become
steadily more humbled by how hard the cultural, data, and statistical problems
actually are. Bayesian inference feels like the right home for this work, because
every algorithm, risk score, and model reflects judgment rather than fact, and I
would rather build tools that say so.

So I started building it. FRESH is my attempt at the infrastructure problem. It is
not finished, and I do not know that I am solving it correctly. I think the question
is the right one, and I would rather work on it in public than wait until I am sure.

## What honest looks like in practice

Saying how sure you are is not a disclaimer bolted on at the end. It changes what
gets built.

So the doubt stays visible on the result, because a number without its uncertainty
is not an answer. Quality never collapses to a single score. When credible expert systems
disagree about the same food, the spread is reported rather than averaged away, and
the food is marked contested rather than quietly assigned a number. Contradictions
between studies get explained before they are declared. Measurement error is carried
from the raw input through to the value on screen. Nothing counts as settled here
until it reproduces a published benchmark, standard error included.

None of that is the point of the platform. It is what makes the point trustworthy.

## The information is already everywhere

Nobody sits down to consult the informational environment. It arrives anyway. It is
the conversation at dinner, the answer you give a child who asks why one cereal is
better than another, the headline you half-read on a phone, the thing a friend
swears worked for them, the label you glance at with a cart in your hand. None of it
announces itself as information. By the time anyone makes a decision, belief has
already taken shape in the background, assembled out of all of it.

That is why pointing at individual choices misreads the problem. Nobody stands
outside the information they grew up inside, experts included. So what people
believe gets measured here with the same seriousness as composition and effect
sizes, then compared against the evidence. The gaps come back specific: foods the
public judges harshly that the evidence treats kindly, foods it lets off easy, and
foods the experts cannot agree on either, which makes public confusion an entirely
reasonable response. Naming which is which is an education agenda, food by food,
rather than a scolding.

## Food first, then the rest of a life

Food comes first because it is the hardest case and the most daily one: expert
systems clash most openly there, measurement is noisiest, and public belief has
drifted furthest from the evidence. The methods are not about food. The same
machinery reaches sleep, movement, mind and mood, social connection and loneliness,
self-care, substance use, biological age, health literacy, and the place you live,
read from what you report, what you wear, and what your blood says.

## What it is made of

Five engines sit behind the tools and essays here. None of them is really about
food.

| Engine | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | Reads the published literature end to end: finds the studies, checks trial quality and trustworthiness, re-pools the effects, and keeps a trail from every claim back to its source. |
| **Consensus** | Reconciles competing expert rating systems into one answer with the disagreement measured and reported, never hidden inside an average. |
| **Risk** | Combines risk models with trial-derived effects to estimate what a change is actually worth for particular people and places, with uncertainty propagated rather than dropped. |
| **Decision** | Turns contradictory signals into one personal answer that shows its own doubt. |
| **Well-being** | Scores well-being across an open set of life domains from self-report, wearable, and biomarker inputs, per domain and combined. |

Together they are meant to do what no single adviser can, which is the framing on
the [front page](index.qmd).

## Who this is for

Anyone who wants to see the evidence for themselves: people making decisions about
their own health, the people who care for them, and the people writing the labels,
the guidance, and the policy. The essays are the argument in public. The tools let
you check it.

If you are thinking about health measurement, clinical risk, nutrition science,
science reform, or what honest evidence synthesis even looks like, I want to hear
from you. So let's start talking better, asking better questions, and building tools
that turn scientific complexity into better health decisions.
